text: Women accounted for almost all of the job growth. All the jobs are going to women. 98% of new jobs in August went to women. Women account for 98% of the jobs that people got last month in August. 98% of jobs are going to women. Men are being pushed out of the workforce. Matriarchy is here. After CNBC and some other major media outlets covered the August jobs report, you could have come across videos with such slogans. So what happened? Yes, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that in August, USA added 162,000 non-farm payroll jobs and women's payroll employment increased by 158,000, 158 divided by 162 is about 98%. So first things first, that number is real. What I'm getting a little tired of is the sensationalism surrounding what that number actually means. Because do you know what happened just two months earlier in June? The economy added 31,000 net payroll jobs. Women's payroll employment increased by 89,000 while men's actually fell by 58,000. So mathematically, women accounted for around 287% of net job growth, 287%. Should the headline have been, women took 287% of all jobs, men are officially finished? And now let's go back to September, 2025. Total payroll employment increased by 76,000. Women accounted for only around 1,000 of that increase, which means men accounted for about 75,000, roughly 99% of net job growth. So what happened? Did the matriarchy get canceled for one month? That's the problem with taking one monthly net change, turning it into a percentage and then building an entire social narrative around it. And notice I keep saying net job growth. This doesn't mean that 158,000 women were hired and only 4,000 men were hired in August. Millions of people can be hired, quit, get fired, retire or change jobs. These numbers are simply the difference between the number of payroll positions at the beginning and the end. Now, I also don't want to overcorrect in the other direction because there is a real trend here. Women have accounted for considerably more of recent payroll growth than men. In the past year, from August, 2025 to August, 2026, U.S. nonfarm payroll employment increased by about 603,000. Women's payroll employment increased by 495,000. That's about 82% of the net increase. And you know what? Great, why can't we acknowledge that this has been a good period for women's employment without immediately turning it into men are doomed or the matriarchy has arrived? Because when you actually look at where the jobs are growing, a lot of this becomes pretty straightforward. Private education and health services added about 539,000 jobs over that year. Women gained about 399,000 jobs in that sector alone. And roughly 77% of the people already working in that sector are women. So if one of the fastest growing parts of the economy is already overwhelmingly female, guess what happens? Women's employment grows faster. That is not particularly mysterious, but there is another reason I don't want you to get hypnotized by the 82% number. Look at women's actual share of all nonfarm payroll jobs. August, 2025, about 50.01%. August, 2026, about 50.13%. So after a year in which women accounted for 82% of all job growth, women's share of payroll employment moved by roughly one-tenth of one percentage point. So the actual composition of the workforce went from basically 50-50 to still basically 50-50. That is the big picture the headline doesn't give you. And are men actually disappearing from the workforce? Not exactly. For adults 20 and older, the August unemployment rate was around 4% for men and 3.5% for women. So yes, women's unemployment rate is currently lower, but men also have a substantially higher labor force participation rate, about 69.4% for men versus 57.9% for women. And the percentage of the adult population actually employed is also much higher for men, about 66.6% versus 55.8%. So there are legitimate differences between men and women in the labor market, but men have basically stopped getting jobs is not a serious description of what is happening. And there's one more important detail hidden inside the phrase nonfarm payrolls. It's called nonfarm because farm workers aren't included. The payroll survey also excludes proprietors, the unincorporated self-employed, unpaid family workers, and private household workers. And some of those excluded groups lean heavily male. For example, in broader household survey in August, there were about 5.2 million male versus 3.7 million female unincorporated self-employed workers outside agriculture. Agricultural wage workers and self-employed farmers were also disproportionately made. So what's the actual conclusion? Yes, women have accounted for most of the net payroll job growth recently. A major reason is that a lot of the growth has happened in industries like healthcare and education, where women already make up a large majority of workers. That is good news for women, but no, men have not suddenly been shut out of the labor market and no, one unusually lopsided month is not evidence that the American economy has entered some kind of matriarchy. Sometimes the statistic isn't wrong, but the story people build around the statistic is.
